growth_story.headline: Twenty years of slow growth ended in 2011; political crisis, then war from 2015, left income per person in 2018 below its 1990 level.
growth_story.arc: From 1991 to 2010 income per person in Yemen grew 1.6 percent a year on average, in an economy the IMF described as heavily dependent on oil, with oil output on a long downward trend. The 2011 political crisis broke that run: unrest and sabotage of oil pipelines cut output, and income per person fell 15.3 percent that year. After a brief steadying, armed conflict began in March 2015 and income per person fell 30.2 percent in a single year. Across 2011 to 2018 growth averaged -8.7 percent a year, and by 2018 income per person was 54.2 percent below its 2010 peak and lower than in 1990. The data stop in 2018, but the sources describe further decline since then, as attacks on oil facilities halted oil exports in 2022, the country split into two economic zones and aid fell.

since_last_year.text: In August 2025 the rial in Aden rose sharply and then held steady, helped by central bank measures and money from abroad, including Saudi support. In April 2026 the IMF resumed its regular reviews of Yemen's economy after a long break, and in October 2026 IMF management approved a staff-monitored program. Both lenders say the war in the Middle East has darkened the outlook, and the IMF now expects output to shrink again in 2026.

growth_story.tension: The data file stops in 2018, when income per person was 54.2 percent below its 2010 peak. The sources describe more years of decline after that, including the halt of oil exports in 2022, so the gap shown here probably understates where income per person stands today. The sources also differ among themselves on recent years: the IMF and the World Bank give different estimates of how much output fell in 2025.
